title: A corner of Argentina has spoken Welsh since 153 settlers landed there in 1865

cover.alt: Capilla Bethel, a small chapel with arched windows and a gabled front, one of the Welsh chapels at Gaiman in Chubut, Argentina.
cover.credit: Ministerio de Cultura de la Nación (Argentina) · CC BY-SA 2.0

body: On 28 July 1865, 153 Welsh settlers came ashore from the clipper Mimosa at the bay now called Puerto Madryn, in Patagonia. The movement’s founder, Michael D. Jones, wanted a colony far from English influence where Welsh could survive as the language of daily life, and Argentina offered land in the Chubut valley on those terms. After a hard start, the settlers traded bread for meat with the Tehuelche people, who also taught them to hunt. Today Welsh is still spoken in towns such as Gaiman, Trelew and Trevelin: estimates range from about 1,500 to 5,000 speakers, and an annual eisteddfod keeps the tradition alive.

slides.prompt: What did the Welsh settlers trade with the Tehuelche?
slides.detail: After early suspicion and some violence, the Tehuelche formed cordial ties with the settlers, helped them through food shortages and taught them to hunt.

slides.heading: Welsh towns of Chubut
items: Rawson: the first settlement, now the provincial capital
Gaiman and Dolavon: centres of the Welsh community
Trelew: hosts the Eisteddfod del Chubut each October
Trevelin and Esquel: the settlements in the Andes

slides.heading: How many speak Welsh in Patagonia?
slides.note: Estimates vary widely; in 2014 Prof. E. Wyn James suggested as many as 5,000

slides.question: Why did the settlers choose remote Patagonia?
options: To keep Welsh alive away from English
slides.explanation: Michael D. Jones proposed a Welsh-speaking colony away from English influence, and Argentina offered land where the settlers could preserve their language and culture.

slides.heading: Still alive
slides.text: Welsh never became the language of the whole region, and Spanish dominates, but it survives in homes and chapels. Estimates of speakers range from about 1,500 to 5,000, and the Eisteddfod, a festival of music and poetry, is held every year.
